'''Sonja Ashauer''' (9 April 1923 – 21 August 1948) was a Brazilian physicist. She was the first Brazilian woman to earn a doctorate in physics, and the second to become a physics graduate in Brazil.<ref name=memoria>{{cite web|title=SONJA ASHAUER (1923 - 1948)|url=http://memoria.cnpq.br/pioneiras-view/-/journal_content/56_INSTANCE_a6MO/10157/902653;jsessionid=C9A8A8C4B643C3848E9A546B6DF95D2B?p_p_state=pop_up&_56_INSTANCE_a6MO_viewMode=print|accessdate=27 October 2016 |language=Portuguese}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://cienciaseadjacencias.blogspot.lu/2011/03/mulheres-na-ciencia-reconhecimentos-e.html|title=Mulheres na ciência: reconhecimentos e esquecimentos |publisher=cienciaseadjacencias.blogspot.lu|accessdate=12 November 2015 |language=Portuguese}}</ref>

==Biography==
Born in [[São Paulo]], Ashauer was the daughter of the [[Germans|German]]-born engineer Walter Ashauer and his wife Herta Graffenbenger who had emigrated to Brazil.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Dahn |first=Ryan |date=2025-07-01 |title=Highlighting women in quantum history |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/highlighting-women-in-quantum-history |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=78 |issue=7 |pages=36–40 |doi=10.1063/pt.cbac.nafv |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref> From 1935 to 1939, she pursued her secondary education at Gymnasium of São Paulo state capital.<ref name=memoria/> Encouraged by her father, after secondary school, she studied physics under [[Gleb Wataghin]] at the [[University of São Paulo]], graduating in 1942. She was the second female physics graduate in Brazil, the first being [[Yolande Monteux]] who graduated in 1938.<ref name=memoria/>

In January 1948, she became the first woman from Brazil to be awarded a doctorate in physics after studying for three years at the [[University of Cambridge]] under the Nobel prizewinner [[Paul Dirac]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Saitovitch |first1=Elisa Maria Baggio |last2=Barbosa |first2=Marcia Cristina |last3=Funchal |first3=Renata Zukanovich |last4=de Pinho |first4=Suani Tavares Rubim |last5=de Santana |first5=Ademir Eugênio |date=2015 |title=Gender equity in the Brazilian physics community at the present time |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.4937654 |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1702 |issue=1 |page=060007 |publisher=AIP Publishing LLC |doi=10.1063/1.4937654|bibcode=2015AIPC.1697f0007S |hdl=10183/159273 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> She was said to have been a brilliant student. Her thesis (''Problems in electrons and electromagnetic radiation)'' explored the cutting-edge field of [[quantum electrodynamics]]. In this research, Ashauer focused on solving the problem that when the electron was modeled as a point source, its [[self-energy]] tended to infinity.<ref name=":0" /> In March 1948, she returned to Brazil, where she was appointed as Wataghin's assistant.<ref name=memoria/>

Ashauer was the first woman from Brazil elected as a member of the Cambridge Philosophical Society.<ref name=memoria/>

Later that year, after catching a cold on a rainy day, she contracted pneumonia. She was taken to hospital, but she died six days later on 21 August 1948. The cause of death stated on the death certificate was "broncopneumonia, myocarditis, and heart failure".<ref name=memoria/>
